# Saṅgāmaji Sutta (Ud 1.8 (PTS Ud 5))

**ID:** Ud 1.8 (PTS Ud 5)
**Section:** Udāna (ud)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Saṅgāmaji Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ud1.8
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0503m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Saṅgāmaji Sutta* (Ud 1.8) is the eighth discourse in the opening chapter (*Bodhivagga*) of the Pali Udāna [SuttaCentral; Anandajoti Bhikkhu 2007]. Set at Jeta's Grove near Sāvatthī, the narrative centers on the monk Saṅgāmaji, whose former wife (*purāṇa-dutiyikā*) seeks him out while he is resting under a tree [Clarke 2014; Anandajoti Bhikkhu 2007; Masefield 1997]. Bearing their young child, she repeatedly demands that he provide support, but Saṅgāmaji remains completely silent [Clarke 2014; Powers 2009]. In a bid to provoke fatherly emotion, she places the infant directly in front of him and leaves, yet Saṅgāmaji neither speaks to nor glances at his offspring [Powers 2009; Bailey and Mabbett 2003; Horner 1930]. Seeing that he is entirely devoid of desire or attachment, she retrieves the child and departs defeated [Bailey and Mabbett 2003; Powers 2009]. Witnessing this encounter with his divine eye, the Buddha breathes forth an inspired utterance (*udāna*) praising Saṅgāmaji: one who neither rejoices when a partner comes nor grieves when she departs, freed from bondage, is a true brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*) [Horner 1930; Bailey and Mabbett 2003; Powers 2009].

Scholars have frequently cited this text in discussions of early Buddhist monastic renunciation, the severance of familial ties, and monastic masculinity [Bailey and Mabbett 2003; Powers 2009; Dhammika 2005]. While the sutta highlights the radical transcendence of household obligations, the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā* elaborates upon Saṅgāmaji's pre-monastic background, directing readers to the *Raṭṭhapāla Sutta* (MN 82) regarding the protracted negotiations required to gain parental consent for ordination [Clarke 2014].

Curated parallels include two Chinese Āgama versions in the *Saṁyuktāgama* (SA 1072) and the 'other' *Saṁyuktāgama* (SA2 11), along with a resembling discourse in *Ekottarāgama* (EA 35.10) [SuttaCentral; Bingenheimer 2011]. The verse corresponds to verse parallels in the Sanskrit and Tibetan *Udānavarga* (UV 33, Uv Kg 33) and the *Chuyaojing* (T 212.34), and the discourse is cited in the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus matches confirm strong cross-language alignment with the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99, fascicle 38), and document internal Pali text-reuse across the *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga* (Bu-Vb Pj 1), the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā*, and several Nikāya suttas [DharmaNexus].
